Fluid buildup Leg swelling caused by fluid buildup in leg tissues is known as peripheral edema. It can be caused by a problem with how blood travels through the body. It also can be caused by a problem with the lymphatic system or the kidneys. Leg swelling isn't always a sign of a heart or circulation problem. You can have swelling due to fluid buildup from being overweight, being inactive, sitting or standing for a long time, or wearing tight stockings or jeans. Factors related to fluid buildup include: 1. Acute kidney injury 2. Cardiomyopathy (problem with the heart muscle) 3. Chemotherapy 4. Chronic kidney disease 5. Chronic venous insufficiency (CVI). Leg veins have a problem returning blood to the heart. 6. Cirrhosis (scarring of the liver) 7. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) 8. Heart failure — a condition in which the heart doesn't pump blood as well as it should. 9. Hormone therapy 10. Lymphedema (blockage in the lymph system) 11. Sitting for a long time, such as during airline flights 19. Standing for a long time 20. fetched_contents.text: Diagnostic approach to lower limb edema Abstract Patients with lower limb edema are frequently referred to vascular specialists for evaluation. Multiple etiologies must be considered and often more than one cause may be present. Notably, the role of lymphatic system regardless of the underlying pathology has been underestimated. A thorough history and physical examination and a carefully considered laboratory and imaging evaluation are critical in differentiating causes. In this opinion article, we propose a diagnostic algorithm that incorporates a systematic approach to the patient with leg swelling and provides an efficient pathway for the differential diagnosis for this problem. Keywords: Chronic venous disease, lymphedema, vascular medicine Introduction Lower limb edema is a common and challenging diagnostic problem often with a significant impact. It is defined as swelling caused by an increase in interstitial fluid that exceeds the capacity of physiologic lymphatic drainage. In most cases it occurs when fluid accumulates in subcutaneous tissues leading to volume expansion, although congenital etiologies and lipedema may result in excessive soft tissue in the lower extremities. Fluid collection can be a result of many etiologies including a range of local or systemic disorders, including infra-inguinal superficial and deep venous reflux, supra and infra inguinal deep vein obstruction, and primary and secondary lymphatic diseases. Although the most likely singular cause of unilateral lower limb edema in individuals over 50 years old is venous disease, the etiology is often multifactorial.1 Symptoms can be debilitating and subsequently impact quality of life with significant costs to society.2–5 Recent work has demonstrated that chronic edema negatively impacts physical and psychological health and reduces quality of life.6 As such, in this opinion article, we propose a practical diagnostic approach to accurately and efficiently identify the causes of chronic edema in affected patients and to institute appropriate therapy. History Lower limb swelling may present to the clinician in several ways. It is essential to take a complete patient history to facilitate accurate, efficient, and cost-effective diagnostic testing and management. The site of swelling and any associated manifestations should be assessed, including whether it is unilateral, bilateral equal or bilateral but asymmetric, along with any changes that occur with its severity with position and time of day. Swelling may be asymptomatic, although it can be associated with symptoms such as aching, pain, heaviness, characteristic venous or lymphatic skin changes or prior or active ulcerations of the lower limb. Patients may describe a sudden onset of limb swelling, a gradual onset or a more long-standing condition. Bilateral but asymmetric cases can have unilateral causes on each leg of different etiologies or varying degrees, or a unilateral cause superimposed on a background of systemic disease. Lymphedema and venous edema can also be bilateral unequal and bilateral equal, although bilateral equal is less common with venous etiologies below the IVC since the disease is often asymmetric at any one point in time. Assessing the duration of symptoms is important, with acute swelling (<72 h) more characteristic of etiologies such as DVT, infection, trauma, exacerbation of a medical condition such as congestive heart failure, or recent medication changes. Chronic swelling may be due to venous insufficiency, lymphatic dysfunction, static foot disorders, or more longstanding medical etiologies. Additionally, swelling due to venous disease typically worsens with dependency during the day and improves with elevation. Venous edema is also commonly associated with complaints of aching, heaviness, or fatigue of the limbs. Focal pain may suggest a musculoskeletal or joint issue. Reflex sympathetic dystrophy (complex regional pain syndrome) must also be considered with a significantly painful chronically swollen limb. fetched_contents.text: Hard Lump Under Skin: Possible Causes and Treatments Lumps, bumps, or growths under your skin aren’t uncommon. A lump can form under your skin for many reasons. Read on to learn more about common causes of hard lumps under your skin and when it’s a good idea to have a lump checked out. Can a hard lump be nothing? Often, lumps are harmless (benign). Specific traits of the lump can sometimes tell you more about possible causes and whether you should contact a medical professional. Harmless bumps don’t need to be treated unless you wish to remove them for cosmetic reasons or they become infected. These include: * Epidermoid cyst: These are twice as common in males and typically don’t develop before puberty. * Lipoma: These are most common in adults 40 to 60 years of age. While they usually don’t need treatment, they may be a symptom of an underlying genetic condition such as Gardner’s syndrome. * Dermatofibroma: While this lump is harmless, it might sometimes itch or hurt. According to research, they are more common in females. * Ganglion cyst: A ganglion cyst is a small, round, fluid-filled lump that grows under the skin’s surface, usually on your hands. The cyst sits on a small stalk that may seem movable. It’s typically harmless and tends to appear most often in people between 15 to 40 years of age. Cause of lumps that may require treatment include: * Keratoacanthoma (KA): This skin tumor is more common in areas with high sun exposure, such as the hands or face. * Skin abscess:This is a round, pus-filled lump most commonly caused by bacterial infections. Treatment often involves drainage and antibiotics. * Swollen lymph nodes: Lymph nodes respond to infections by trapping and eliminating damaged or infectious cells. Lymphocytes can cause swelling in the nodes as part of the immune response. This can also be caused by injury and, in some cases, cancer. The treatment depends on the cause. * Hernia: This is a lump that develops when part of your body, such as one of your organs, pushes through the surrounding tissue. There are several types of hernias. Pictures How are hard lumps diagnosed? Doctors can usually diagnose benign skin tumors by looking at their location, appearance, and additional features, such as whether it hurts, itches, or bleeds. If there is any doubt or the tumor starts to change unexpectedly, you may need to have it removed and analyzed with a biopsy. Your doctor may also order imaging, such as an MRI, CT scan, or ultrasound. When should I be concerned about a hard lump? Often, hard lumps don’t require medical treatment. But it’s always a good idea to talk with a healthcare professional like a dermatologist if you experience growths on your skin that change shape, color, or size. Typically, a non-cancerous lump will have a soft texture and be able to move under the skin. So if you notice a hard lump, see a doctor for a proper diagnosis. That said, cancerous lumps may also be soft. Also see a doctor if the lump: * bleeds or leaks * causes pain * grows larger * becomes red or inflamed * is accompanied by unintentional weight loss Takeaway Lumps under the skin are very common and can have a range of causes. In some cases, lumps go away without treatment. It’s not always possible to tell exactly what causes a lump. If you notice a lump under your skin, keep an eye on it. In general soft, movable lumps are harmless and may improve with time. That said, it’s always a good idea to make an appointment with a healthcare professional, especially if you’re worried.

## How to distinguish swelling from a lump

The key distinction between swelling and a solid bump lies in the underlying pathophysiology and the way the physical exam findings relate to the patient’s symptoms. Swelling is usually fluid accumulation in tissues, while a lump is more often a discrete, palpable mass of tissue or fluid-filled structure [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F4]. The Mayo Clinic guide on leg swelling emphasizes that a thorough history and physical examination are critical to differentiate causes, and that the same applies to examining a lump [N2-F2][N2-R2]. In practical terms, the physical exam should focus on whether the change is diffuse, localized, firm, mobile, tender, or associated with other findings such as redness, warmth, or skin changes [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F4].

### Physical exam features that help tell swelling from a solid bump

A useful starting point is the appearance of the affected area. Swelling is typically described as a diffuse, soft, or pitting increase in volume, especially in the legs [N2-R3][N2-R4][N4-F4]. In contrast, a solid bump is usually a discrete, palpable structure that may feel firm or hard and is often not associated with widespread tissue expansion [N4-F4]. The diagnostic approach to lower limb edema also highlights that swelling is often accompanied by symptoms such as heaviness, pain, or aching, and that focal pain may suggest a musculoskeletal or joint issue [N2-F2]. For a lump, inspection and palpation are both important, and the physical exam should include whether the mass is movable, fixed, tender, or associated with skin changes such as redness or warmth [N2-R2][N4-F4].

### How location, shape, mobility, and skin changes differ between the two

Location is one of the strongest clues. Leg swelling is more likely to be generalized or involve the entire limb, especially if it worsens with dependence or improves with elevation [N2-F2]. In contrast, a lump is typically localized and may appear on a specific area of the leg, such as a bony prominence, soft tissue, or near a vein [N4-F4]. Shape also differs: swelling is usually round or irregular and not sharply defined, whereas a lump may have a more definite border [N2-R2][N4-F4]. Mobility is another key difference. Swelling may be nonmobile or only partially mobile because it involves interstitial fluid and surrounding tissue; a lump may be mobile, fixed, or partially mobile depending on its origin [N2-R2][N4-F4]. Skin changes are especially important: pitting, redness, warmth, or erythema are more consistent with swelling, particularly if they suggest inflammation, infection, or fluid overload [N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R2][N4-F4].

### When imaging or other tests are useful to clarify the diagnosis

Imaging or other tests are useful when the diagnosis is unclear or when red flags are present. The diagnostic approach to lower limb edema explicitly states that a carefully considered laboratory and imaging evaluation are critical in differentiating causes [N2-F2]. For a leg lump, the Healthline article notes that doctors may use imaging such as MRI, CT scan, or ultrasound if there is doubt or if the lump changes unexpectedly [N4-F4]. Similarly, the Mayo Clinic guidance on leg swelling advises seeking care if symptoms are sudden, painful, or associated with systemic signs such as chest pain, difficulty breathing, or shortness of breath [N3-F3]. In practice, this means that when the patient has redness, warmth, pain, or a rapid onset, imaging and specialist evaluation may be warranted [N2-R4][N3-F3][N4-F4].

## Bottom line

If the patient’s leg problem is a general swelling, it is likely to be diffuse, soft, and associated with fluid-related symptoms; if it is a solid bump, it is more likely to be a discrete, palpable mass that may be firm or movable [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F4]. The most important clues are location, shape, mobility, skin changes, and whether the change is acute or chronic [N2-F2][N4-F4]. Imaging or specialist evaluation becomes especially helpful when the findings are unclear, when there is redness or warmth, or when the patient has concerning symptoms such as sudden onset or pain [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4].

## What the patient should tell the physician next to narrow the diagnosis

The physician needs a clear, structured account of the patient’s symptoms, timing, and associated features to narrow the diagnosis. The evidence supports that a thorough history and physical examination are essential for leg swelling and lumps alike [N2-F2][N2-R2]. In practical terms, the patient should describe the bump and swelling in a way that answers several key questions: when it started, how it changed over time, whether it is tender, whether it is warm or red, and whether it is getting worse [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4]. The patient should also mention any prior injury, recent travel, medications, or underlying conditions, because these can change the differential diagnosis [N3-F3][N5-R1][N5-R2].

### Specific questions to ask the physician about symptoms and history

The patient should ask the physician:

- **When did the swelling or bump first appear?**  
  Acute versus chronic timing changes the likely diagnosis [N2-F2][N6-R3].

- **Has it gotten bigger, or has it changed in shape, color, or texture?**  
  Change is a red flag that may point to infection, inflammation, or a growing mass [N4-F4][N3-F3].

- **Is it tender, painful, warm, or red?**  
  Pain, warmth, and redness are strongly suggestive of infection, inflammation, or acute edema [N2-R2][N2-R4][N2-R5][N3-F3].

- **Does it improve when elevated, rest, or move?**  
  This can help distinguish venous versus lymphatic or inflammatory causes [N2-F2][N5-R2].

- **Have you had any injury, recent surgery, or travel?**  
  These can trigger blood clots, trauma, or deep vein thrombosis [N3-F3][N5-R1].

- **Do you have other symptoms?**  
  The physician should ask about fever, weight loss, chest pain, shortness of breath, or changes in urine or bowel habits, because these may point to systemic illness [N3-F3][N2-F2][N4-F4].

- **Do you take any medications?**  
  Some medications can cause leg swelling or lumps as side effects [N1-F1][N3-F3].

### What information is most helpful for deciding whether to see a doctor

The most helpful information is the **timing and pattern** of the change, because acute onset is more concerning than chronic or slowly progressive swelling [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The patient should also report whether the change is **localized or widespread**, whether it is **firm or soft**, and whether it is **associated with skin changes such as redness, warmth, or pitting** [N2-F2][N2-R3][N4-F4]. The patient should also note whether the bump is **moving under the skin or fixed**, because mobility can help distinguish benign from more serious conditions [N4-F4].

### How to describe the bump, swelling, and soreness clearly

The patient should describe the bump and swelling in a way that captures both appearance and behavior:

- **Location**: “It’s on the inside/back of my mom’s leg,” or “it’s near the ankle.”
- **Size and shape**: “It’s a small bump, about the size of a pea,” or “the swelling is on one side and looks like it’s spreading.”
- **Texture**: “It feels soft,” “firm,” “hard,” “moveable,” or “fixed.”
- **Color and skin changes**: “The skin is red,” “warm,” or “not red.”
- **Soreness and pain**: “It’s a bit sore, but not too bad,” “it hurts when touched,” or “it’s painful when she walks.”
- **Timing and change**: “It started two days ago,” “it’s gotten a little worse,” or “it hasn’t changed much.”
- **Associated symptoms**: “She has a little fever,” “she has chest pain,” or “she’s been sitting a lot.”

## Bottom line

To narrow the diagnosis, the patient should tell the physician when the swelling or bump started, whether it has changed over time, whether it is tender, warm, red, or pitting, and whether it is localized or generalized [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4]. The patient should also report any prior injury, recent travel, medications, and other symptoms because these can change the likely diagnosis [N3-F3][N5-R1][N5-R2]. The clearest description is one that captures location, texture, color, pain, and timing, along with any associated systemic symptoms [N2-F2][N4-F4].

## Most likely explanations

### 1) Benign causes are common

The evidence suggests that many leg bumps are harmless. Benign skin lumps such as **epidermoid cysts, lipomas, dermatofibromas, and ganglion cysts** are common and often do not need treatment unless they change, become infected, or are cosmetically bothersome [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-F4].

- **Cellulitis**, an acute skin infection, can cause **pain, warmth, swelling, and redness** [N1-R2][N2-R5].
- **Trauma or injury** can lead to a bump and swelling, especially if the patient has recently fallen, strained her leg, or had a minor injury [N3-F3].
